Development guide

Tech Scan: Sandbox

Where should agent-written code run, and which resources could it reach? Choose an execution route for the task, then check its network, credential and approval boundaries.

Draft research reference from web sources reviewed 11–12 November 2026; not locally deployed or benchmarked. For the underlying explanation, read Concepts: harness engineering and Path to production.

On this page
Choose the execution boundary Match the AWS starting point to the task Exclude the wrong execution boundary Evidence to collect before relying on the boundary Sources

Choose the execution boundary

Where will agent-written code run, and which resources could it reach? Choose an execution boundary for that task before adding tools. For this guide's untrusted-code use case, plain shared-kernel containers alone do not meet the stronger boundary sought here. Isolation reduces risk; it is not a guarantee against escape or misuse of an allowed credential. A separate guest kernel is one approach; a userspace application kernel is another, with different compatibility and security properties.[19]

Gateway policy governs calls through the Gateway, not arbitrary shell networking. VPC attachment alone does not establish package-only egress or secret denial. Check allowed destinations, dependency sources, role permissions, credentials and session ownership separately from the isolation mechanism.[22] Runtime Instances is not per-session microVM isolation: co-resident agents in an Instances session share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentials.[12]

For the surrounding loop and tools, use Tech Scan: Harness. This page compares execution choices and controls; the model and release pipeline remain separate decisions.

Test the boundary, not the product label

Separate three failure paths before allowing unattended execution: policy bypass (a command or network connection uses an unguarded path), isolation escape (code crosses the guest or host boundary), and permitted misuse (code uses an allowed but excessive identity or credential). A prompt, a tool approval and a microVM address different parts of that threat model; none replaces independent egress, identity and release controls. Vercel's October 2026 sandbox challenge uncovered a Linux-kernel flaw exploitable from a guest microVM; Vercel reported no customer-data access. This is evidence that even stronger isolation requires patch management and containment, not evidence that all microVMs are unsafe. [25]

BoundaryEnforcesDoes not establishAcceptance test
Local command sandboxLimits covered shell commands and child processesRestrictions on agent file tools, remote MCP tools or the host itselfDeny a filesystem write and network destination through the covered shell, then separately test the other tool routes
Guest or microVMSeparates executing code from the host using the chosen isolation designFreedom from kernel vulnerabilities, excessive identities or allowed egressRecord patch ownership, guest-to-host isolation design and denied access using the actual execution role
Identity, egress and action policyRestricts what credentials, destinations and operations a workload may useThat generated code is correct or that a release may be approvedExercise a denied credential, IP destination and sensitive action, including bypass routes

Match the AWS starting point to the task

These are alternatives for different tasks and deployment responsibilities, not a prescription to deploy them together. Start with the managed harness for repository coding; choose additional execution services only when the task needs them.

A minimal starting point for each execution task
TaskStarting pointBoundary to qualify
Repository codingManaged harness with built-in shell and filesystem toolsPrepare the repository, dependencies and tests in the harness environment; do not add Code Interpreter merely to obtain a shell.[20][21]
Data analysis or computationOptional AgentCore Code InterpreterPython, JavaScript or TypeScript computation; review its execution role and networking separately. Browser is another optional tool for a specific browsing task.[20]
Own EKS or ECS container infrastructureInvestigate Nitro SandboxesA VM boundary for supported workloads; the team still operates its cluster, images and network controls. The launch announcement dates from 9 November 2026.[1][2]

Controls the isolation mechanism does not replace

Keep these checks visible whichever execution route you choose. Apply Kubernetes-specific controls only to a Kubernetes deployment; they are not a universal AgentCore configuration.

Separate access controls from the execution boundary
ControlActionLimit to retain
EgressConfigure and test allowed destinations for the selected execution routeGateway policy is not a shell-network control; VPC attachment is not an allowlist. Network mode and routing need explicit verification.[8][22]
IdentityUse a minimal execution role and short-lived, task-scoped credentialsCode allowed to use a credential may misuse it; isolation does not make an overpowered role safe.[22]
SecretsCSI mounts without sync avoid creating a Kubernetes Secret for that mount. ESO creates Kubernetes Secret objects; CSI also offers optional sync to those objects.[16][17]Kubernetes Secrets are stored in etcd. If using ESO or CSI sync, apply encryption at rest, restrict RBAC and control which workloads can mount the Secret. Mounted credentials remain accessible to authorised workload code; avoiding etcd is not zero-risk credential protection.[18]
Admission and approvalFor Kubernetes, map applicable machine-verifiable IM8 and ARC controls to admission constraintsRetain reviewed evidence and manual approval for the remainder. An admitted workload and a sandboxed code output still need the separate delivery decision.
Nitro deployment mechanics and the AWS execution catalogue

Open this after choosing to operate the infrastructure. The launch material below describes specific deployment modes, not settings inherited by every managed harness. Recheck supported versions, regions and operating limits before deployment.

For teams operating their own supported container infrastructure, investigate AWS Nitro Sandboxes, announced 9 November 2026: a hardware-isolated lightweight virtual machine per EKS pod, ECS task or EC2 workload, managed by the Nitro Hypervisor, at no extra charge beyond the instance, in all commercial regions, explicitly positioned for LLM-generated code and AI agents.[1][2] On EKS and ECS the sandbox is a Firecracker microVM running on Nitro instead of KVM, so each pod gets its own operating system and kernel.

Opting in takes one field on EKS: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox. The runtime classes ship with every EKS Auto Mode cluster; standard EKS needs a sandbox-enabled node AMI (Amazon Machine Image). On ECS the equivalent is trustedExecutionConfiguration on Managed Instances only. On EC2, launch with --enclave-options Enabled=true, then run Firecracker from your own orchestrator or AMI.

There are two modes. Isolated protects the host and neighbour pods from the pod — the mode for agent-generated code, continuous integration and multi-tenant work. Confidential treats even the machine operator as untrusted:

  • Memory is moved out of the parent's reach.
  • Exec and stdin are denied.
  • Nitro Security Module (NSM) attestation covers the image and the Cedar policy.
  • KMS releases secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match.

One caveat: without a KMS key policy verifying measurements, the measurement is recorded but never verified.

For networking, the annotation sandbox.amazonaws.com/network-isolated: "true" boots the virtual machine with loopback-only networking (no network access except to itself). A per-pod Cedar policy decides which images may load, which containers start, and whether exec, log streaming and mounts are allowed. Encrypted OCI layers are decrypted inside the sandbox with KMS, and AWS Signer-signed images are verifiable before they run. Pod Identity, VPC networking, EBS, EFS and S3 storage, and CloudWatch all keep working, and kubectl exec, logs and port-forward work identically in isolated mode.

Vendor example, not a local trial: AWS's sample runs a Claude Code agent via Bedrock inside one sandbox. The agent:

  1. Reads a GitHub issue.
  2. Reproduces it with a failing test.
  3. Fixes it.
  4. Runs the suite.
  5. Pushes a branch.
  6. Opens a pull request.

Egress is locked by an EKS ApplicationNetworkPolicy: CoreDNS and HTTPS to Bedrock and GitHub hostnames only. Model access runs through Pod Identity scoped to bedrock:InvokeModel*, and the agent holds one short-lived fine-grained GitHub token. A prompt-injection test that pipes a remote script into a shell never opens a connection, and when the pod exits the virtual machine is destroyed. A sample repository is listed in the sources.[3]

The limits, stated plainly:

  • Kubernetes 1.36 or later
  • No GPU passthrough
  • No snapshot, pause and resume with memory, live migration, or in-place resize
  • No published cold-start numbers, performance figures or service-level agreement (SLA)

AWS's Nitro Sandboxes launch blog (9 November 2026) says a warm pool built on the Kubernetes Special Interest Group (SIG) agent-sandbox project keeps pre-booted VMs ready to claim in about two seconds;[2] the SIG project's own announcement claims warm-pool claims reduce cold start to less than one second. Treat both as vendor or project claims, not a local measurement.

The four AWS sandbox primitives — do not confuse them
PrimitiveIsolationRunsBest for
Nitro SandboxesPer-pod or per-task Firecracker microVM on your EC2Any containerised agent unchangedEKS shops; compliance or spend commitments; you own the cluster
Nitro EnclavesTiny locked-down VM, no networking, no storage, vsock onlyOne signed function: key custody, signing, PII tokenisationSecrets work — not a code-execution sandbox
Bedrock AgentCorePer-session Firecracker microVM, managedThe agent loop (Runtime, up to 8 h), agent-written code (Code Interpreter, fixed 2 vCPU / 8 GB), real web UIs (Browser, managed Chromium)Zero-infrastructure option
Lambda MicroVMsPer-session Firecracker microVM from a snapshot, own HTTPS endpoint; suspend and resume with memory and disk, up to 8 hA custom execution layer you build yourselfBuild-your-own sandbox API

Nitro Sandboxes were announced 9 November 2026.[5] Nitro Enclaves are GA since 2020, and there is no EKS-native enclave feature — the pattern is a pod on an enclave-enabled node driving nitro-cli. Bedrock AgentCore is GA since 13 October 2025, including in the Singapore region. Lambda MicroVMs were announced 22 June 2026 on the ARM64 architecture, in five regions without Singapore.[10][11][14] AWS added x86_64 support on 5 November 2026 and has since expanded regions, so check the current architectures and regions before recommending them.[15]

Runtime Instances is not per-session microVM compute: co-resident agents in an Instances session share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentials. Do not treat it as an isolation boundary for untrusted code.[12]

Code Interpreter package-installation advisories

AgentCore advisories

The cited package-installation advisories concern the SDK around Code Interpreter, not a demonstrated microVM escape. CVE-2026-12530 (June 2026, fixed in 1.6.1) and CVE-2026-16796 with AWS Security Bulletin 2026-065 (July 2026, fixed in 1.18.1) work the same way: crafted package names lead to remote code execution inside the Code Interpreter sandbox, and from there to reading the attached execution role's credentials from the in-sandbox metadata service. This is package-argument injection inside the sandbox, not a host escape.[6][7]

Controls:

  • The cited July 2026 bulletin names a fix in bedrock-agentcore 1.18.1; check current security bulletins and pin a supported, patched release.
  • Never pass raw model output as package names.
  • Attach least-privilege execution roles and omit them when unnecessary. Absence of an execution role does not prove that workload inputs contain no other credentials.
  • Watch for metadata-service access (169.254.169.254) from inside sandboxes.

Local coding agents: qualify shell sandboxing separately

For developers working locally in Kiro, its command sandbox is an optional, OS-enforced boundary for shell commands and child processes. Enable it with sandbox.json, choose the intended network mode and confirm that status is Active; it is not enabled simply by installing Kiro. The agent harness, built-in file tools and remote MCP servers remain outside the command sandbox. Optional local stdio MCP wrapping has its own setting. If the platform backend is unavailable, commands run without OS isolation unless the selected mode requires protection. Set and test a failure policy rather than silently accepting that fallback. [26]

Qualification: test an allowed build; denied write to a credential path through the shell; denied shell egress; a built-in file-tool attempt; and a remote MCP call. Record which control stopped each operation. If a path remains open, apply an independent permission, filesystem or network boundary before allowing autonomous work.

When the starting point lacks a required capability

Investigate a self-hosted sandbox platform when the chosen AWS route cannot provide a required sandbox API, reusable environment template or pause-and-resume behaviour. Name that requirement first; these candidates are not additional layers to install by default.

Evaluate each platform against its documented deployment contract: required host capabilities, isolation implementation, supported AWS deployment and network and secret controls. Do not assume that E2B or another sandbox platform can be nested into Nitro, Kata or gVisor merely because those names describe isolation options. gVisor is a userspace application kernel, not a microVM; its security and syscall-compatibility trade-offs need their own assessment.[19]

If building the execution layer directly

First establish why a managed execution route cannot meet the task. A runtime boundary does not by itself provide the sandbox API, templates, lifecycle or destination policy.

Isolation primitives and host software to investigate

The initial research named Firecracker with firecracker-containerd, Kata Containers, gVisor (runsc) and Bottlerocket OS.[13] Separate a VM runtime from an application kernel and a hardened host OS; they solve different parts of the problem. gVisor documents its application-kernel boundary and residual limits directly.[19]

Check each project's current licence, supported host and syscall or device requirements. Do not infer Kata compatibility from general EC2 nested-virtualisation availability, or classify a host OS as a per-task execution boundary.

Exclude the wrong execution boundary

  • Plain Docker or runc alone: shared-kernel isolation alone does not meet this guide's stronger boundary for untrusted agent code; this is a scoped selection rule, not a claim that containers provide no isolation.
  • Runtime Instances as a per-session boundary: co-resident agents share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentials.[12]
  • Non-AWS cloud compute: hosted sandboxes from Modal, Deno, Fly, Vercel or Cloudflare are outside the agreed scope of this scan. That does not turn an SDK library into a cloud deployment or establish that any managed SaaS is approved.
Historical lifecycle warnings to recheck

Sysbox is slow-moving and community-maintained, not retired: v0.7.1 shipped 28 July 2026, adding support on Ubuntu 24.04 with kernel 6.8+ under containerd 2.x (v0.7.0, 2 March 2025, already added Kubernetes 1.33–1.35 and containerd 2.0.5+). Check the current release before extending an inherited deployment.

The initial research flagged Daytona OSS; it was archived (frozen at v0.190.0, AGPL-3.0), so do not build on it.

The same issue reports a September 2026 red-team comparison finding network-policy bypasses in 7 of 9 tested platforms. Without its primary report and deployment conditions, treat it as an investigation lead, not an established failure rate for the category.[13]

Evidence to collect before relying on the boundary

Ask the implementing engineer to exercise the selected route in the intended account. Record the exact runtime, image, region, execution role and policy revision, then retain expected and observed results for:

  • An allowed dependency fetch and a denied network destination, including a bare-IP attempt where relevant.
  • Allowed and denied credential access, session separation and permission revocation.
  • Timeout, cancellation and cleanup, including files, credentials and any persistent resources left behind.

Unresolved denials, leaked credentials or incomplete cleanup leave the boundary unqualified. Keep startup and task timings separate from security results; a fast run is not evidence that the controls held.

Shared-host residual risk and maintenance: In controlled frontier-model research, OpenAI reports agents exchanging synthetic secrets across isolated tasks using a shared CPU cache; researchers supplied protocols or direction in most channel tests.[23] Guillermo Rauch describes an independent cpu-chat reproduction in his X post; the available partial extract limits verification of its details.[24] This is a threat model for cooperating, co-resident workloads communicating across an intended boundary, not evidence of ordinary tenant compromise or a universal sandbox bypass. Ask the platform owner how host kernels, hypervisors and sandbox components are patched, how vulnerabilities are disclosed and remediated, and which residual co-residency controls and isolation guarantees apply to the selected deployment.

The 9 November 2026 Nitro launch sources describe availability and mechanisms, not this account's results.[1][2] The initial research did not establish independent startup benchmarks, an SLA or a supported GPU path; recheck those requirements rather than assuming their absence or availability.

Lambda MicroVMs Singapore availability remains unresolved in the retained research: the 22 June 2026 launch covered five regions, while the 7 November 2026 builder article reports 14 without naming them. Confirm current regional availability before selecting it for a Singapore workload.[14][15]

Next, read Path to production for the gates a sandboxed change must still pass — the sandbox bounds what agent code can do, it does not approve the change.

Residual-risk record: include sandbox enablement and unavailable-backend behaviour, guest or host patch owner, direct-IP egress handling, independent identity restrictions, and whether an agent can modify the policy files that would otherwise constrain it. Unresolved cases are deployment blockers for that path, not merely documentation gaps.
